$comment: The parameters of every tool operation, and the sentence a model reads when it gets one wrong. Hand-written: this is the specification, and it covers the catalogue exhaustively — `every_catalog_operation_declares_its_parameters` fails if an operation is added without an entry here. `scripts/generate-command-surface.mjs` emits the Rust table that refuses a call, the signature the model is shown, and the addon-side guard for the operations the addon answers.
$commandComment: `command` is the addon command that answers the operation, and its absence — with `answeredBy: "rust"` in its place — means the operation never reaches the addon. Those are checked in Rust and deserialize into a typed request behind it; `every_rust_answered_operation_matches_its_request` holds this file to those structs.
$summaryComment: `summary` is what the model reads about the operation, one sentence or several, and it is the half of the tool description a person writes. It lives here rather than in Rust because everything else about the same operation already did — the parameters it takes, what answers it, where it may sit in an `ops` list, whether the user is asked first — and the worker is sent one object per operation carrying all of it. Written apart, the view the model receives was assembled at serialization time out of two files nothing held together, and a test had to read English out of Rust source to check the seam.
$acceptsComment: `accepts` names a parameter the addon reads and the model is never told about. `scene` is the only one: every node command takes it and defaults it to the scene the editor already has open, so the desktop client passes it and the model has no reason to.
$gatedComment: `gated` is the sentence the user is shown before the agent may run this operation. Its absence means auto-allowed, so a new operation is allowed by default and has to be gated deliberately. It lives beside the parameters and the route because all three are facts about the same operation, and keeping the safety model in a table of its own meant a fifth place to look and a fifth thing to hold to the catalogue afterwards.
$writesComment: `writes` names what an operation writes where one of the user's enforced Godot rules may refuse it: `projectSetting` and `editorSetting` are the two settings surfaces, `scriptText` is a call carrying GDScript source. `godot_policy::enforcement_refusal` reads the tag rather than matching on the tool and the operation, so an operation renamed here cannot quietly stop being enforced. Absence means no rule keys on this operation — which is every operation but five.
$resultComment: `result` is the shape of the answer an operation succeeds with, in the same vocabulary as `params` and never shown to the model. The generator emits a Rust struct per addon command from it, and `godot_rpc` deserializes every answer into that struct in a debug build — so a declaration that disagrees with the handler is a failed acceptance run rather than a stale sentence. A kind of `shape` names a row of `shapes` below; an `object` with no `entry` is one this codebase does not shape at all — a settings map, a language server payload — and says so by being open.
$aloneComment: `alone` narrows where an operation may sit in an `ops` list, and carries the sentence a caller reads when it gets that wrong. Every tool call is a list, so a model wanting three inspections writes one call rather than three. `scope: "repeat"` is the ordinary case: the operation may sit beside other operations, and may not appear twice, because it takes no parameters to vary or drives something the session owns exactly one of — the open scene, the running game, the undo stack, the dialog. The router runs a list in order, so a second one would only redo or undo the first. `scope: "exclusive"` is the debugger, where each answer decides what the next operation means, so the operation has to be the only entry of its call. Absence means the operation may appear as often as a list names it.
$vocabularyComment: `vocabularies` names a set of words a parameter accepts where `kind` cannot reach — `key` sits inside each entry of an `events` list — and it names them by pointing at a list in `protocol/godot-vocabulary.json`, which is written by running the pinned engine. Nothing here is hand-listed: the twenty-five key names that used to be were a quarter of the hundred and ninety the engine has, and the only thing holding them to it was a test feeding them to a real editor one at a time. The generator resolves `engine` into the words, emits them as the schema `enum` the sampler is constrained by, and the prose says nothing about them: an enum permits and prose steers, and the same enum with a stale list beside it measured worse than with none.
$domainsComment: `domains` is the ten groupings the hundred operations are offered as, and the sentence the model reads about each. It is a decision about presentation rather than a fact about an operation, which is why it is a block of its own — but it is prose the model reads, so it lives where every other sentence it reads lives and the same checks reach it. `ai_tools.rs` CATALOG is generated from this, in this order.

domains.name: godot_session
domains.description: Owns the managed Godot editor session bound to the active task worktree.

domains.name: godot_scene
domains.description: The edited scene in the editor — never the running game's scene tree. Every mutation here is checked against the scene's revision, and the router supplies that number from the last answer that carried one, so never pass it and never read the tree to fetch it.

domains.name: godot_node
domains.description: Node authoring inside the edited scene. Every mutation is undoable and every one of them is checked against the scene's revision — which the router supplies from the last answer that carried one, and every mutation's own answer carries the next. So mutate, then mutate again: there is no revision to pass and no tree to re-read between them. Paths are the scene's own, like /Level1 or /Level1/Ground. Nothing here writes the file: scene.save does.

domains.name: godot_project
domains.description: Project settings, autoloads, the Input Map, plugins, and machine-wide editor settings. Project writes persist in the task worktree; editor settings are machine-wide and outside Git.

domains.name: godot_resource
domains.description: Project files as the editor sees them. Deleting and moving need the user's approval; nothing outside the task worktree can be named at all.

domains.name: godot_script
domains.description: GDScript editing and intelligence through Godot's language server. Positions are {line, character}, zero-based. Open a script before querying it — and write GDScript here rather than with the file tools, which refuse a .gd, because writing here is what tells the server whether it parses. A script that does not parse stops the scene using it from loading. `edit` changes a script that exists and answers with its diagnostics, so it needs no `diagnostics` call after it; `save` creates one, and `diagnostics` on the same path is what then says whether it parses. Paths may be named either way, `scripts/mario.gd` or res://scripts/mario.gd.

domains.name: godot_debug
domains.description: Godot's debug adapter. Install breakpoints with the launch itself, then wait for a stop before inspecting: stopping is an event, not a response.

domains.name: godot_runtime
domains.description: The running game: its live scene tree, input, performance, and screenshots. Distinct from the edited scene, and named differently: every path here starts at /root, where the node.* operations' start at the edited scene's own root.

domains.name: godot_logs
domains.description: The session's captured output — editor, importer, plugin, and the game the editor launched — with a cursor and severity filtering.

domains.name: godot_docs_search
domains.description: The Godot 4.7 documentation, on this machine. SEARCH IT BEFORE writing a class, method, signal or constant name, and before answering any question about how the engine behaves. Do not answer either from memory and do not reason it out from the name: what you remember is mostly Godot 3, where a great many of these names were spelled differently, and a name this does not return is a name to check rather than to guess at. Passages cite a chapter, never a URL. It holds the engine's documentation and nothing else, so send a question about this project's own scripts, scenes or files to the subagent tool instead.

godotKeyName.note: Godot's own name for a key, not the browser's.

godotMonitorName.note: A `Performance.Monitor` constant, as the engine spells it.

godotValueTag.note: The `type_string` spelling of every Variant type a JSON payload can be built into, plus `Resource` for the {path} payload.

godotJoyButton.note: A `JoyButton` constant, as the engine spells it.

godotJoyAxis.note: A `JoyAxis` constant, as the engine spells it.

To build on an existing scene, instantiate it with node.instantiate and set on the instance whatever differs — measured on 4.7.2, the instance keeps what is set on it and the scene it came from is unchanged.

operations.summary: Inspects a node. Answers with its type, its groups, every signal it can emit, the connections it already has, and every property whose value is not still the one its class ships with. The rest are named, without their values, in `atClassDefault` — a Label has 129 properties and four of them differ, so this is most of the node. `properties` narrows the answer to the names you list and answers every one of them in full, at their default or not, exactly as runtime.inspect_node does for the running game. Read a property here before setting it rather than guessing what it holds; `stored` is false for properties the scene recomputes, like a Control's position and size and every theme_override_*, and those are set the same way as any other.

operations.summary: Sets properties, as one revision and one undo step. Each `properties` entry names a node, a property and a value, and entries may name different nodes. `value` is tagged with its type — a `type` beside a `value`: {"type": "Vector2", "value": [12, 34]}, {"type": "float", "value": 1.5}, {"type": "String", "value": "hi"}. A property that holds a resource — a CollisionShape2D's `shape`, a Sprite2D's `texture` — takes {"type": "Resource", "value": {"path": "res://…"}}, never a string: a path written as a string is refused. A property that holds another node — an @export node reference — takes {"type": "NodePath", "value": "Box/Slider"}, a path read from the node the property is on. A color takes four numbers, or a name like "skyblue", or a hex string like "#8b5a2b". The other tags, and the payload each one takes, are the branches the schema lists. Nothing is written unless every entry is accepted.

This is how a 2D level is built — one TileMapLayer carrying a tileset, rather than a node per block. `x`/`y` are cell coordinates, not pixels, and `width`/`height` default to 1 so a rectangle is one entry — a whole ground row is {"x": 0, "y": 12, "width": 200, "height": 2, "atlas": [0, 0]}. `atlas` is the [column, row] of the tile in the tileset, which resource.describe_tileset lists. An entry with no `atlas` erases the cells it covers. The node needs its `tile_set` property set first, with node.set_property and a resource value.

Answers with the atlas grid it found. Build a tileset with this rather than writing one as text: a TileSet carries a record per tile and a polygon per solid one, and a hand-written one opens as a resource with no tiles in it.

A colour is a name or a hex string — "skyblue", "#8b5a2b". An atlas is one texture with a rectangle per tile, laid out on the grid create_tileset then cuts: two 16x16 tiles side by side is a 32x16 image. The texture is imported by the time this answers, so it needs no rescan and create_tileset can name it straight away. Draw art with this rather than through bash: an image library is not something every machine has.

operations.summary: Reports an in-memory buffer change.

Changes existing scripts by replacing exact text, and answers with each file's diagnostics. Put every change to one file in that file's `edits`, and every file in one call: this is one call, not one per change. `oldText` must appear exactly once in the file, so extend it with a neighbouring line when it would not; it is quoted from the file, so read the file first. Either every file is written or none is. To create a script, use `save`.

params.name: files
params.note: Every `oldText` must match one region of that file exactly and must not overlap another edit of the same file. Entries may name different files, and either every file is written or none is.

entry.name: diagnostics

operations.summary: Writes a whole file and answers with the file's diagnostics, the same way `edit` does. Use it to create a script, or to replace one outright; to change part of one, `edit` is the call, and it does not send the file back. A file that already exists is only written over what you have read, so open it first — the router holds the hash that read answered with. A script you are creating needs no read. `update` does not write anything: it reports a buffer change to the language server, and this is the call that puts it on disk. Do not follow this with a `diagnostics` call about the same file: the verdict is already here. `published: false` means the server had not spoken about the text yet, which is not the same as the file being clean.

operations.summary: Returns the running game's scene tree, and `paused`: whether the tree is paused right now. That one belongs to the SceneTree rather than to any node, so `inspect_node` cannot reach it and this is the only call that reports it.

params.name: root
params.note: The node to start from, as a path. The whole tree when it is absent.

params.name: depth
params.note: How many levels below the starting node to walk. Every level when it is absent.

params.name: limit
params.note: How many nodes to answer with, at most. The answer opens with `truncated`, which says whether it stopped early; a root or a depth is how you read the rest.

operations.summary: Inspects a running node. `properties` is the list of property names to read, like ["position", "velocity"]; without it the answer carries the node's path, name and type and an empty property map, so name what you want to see. A name the node does not have is an error rather than a gap. The groups it is in come back whether or not anything was named, because a group is not a property and a script joining one at run time is how half of them are joined.

params.name: path
params.note: The node to read, by its path in the running tree: every one of those starts at /root. The node.* operations call this same thing `node`, and this is the one operation in this catalogue where `path` names a node rather than a file.

entry.name: properties
entry.note: Keyed by property name, and only the ones the call asked for.

operations.summary: Injects input and captures the result. Each event names its kind and the parameters that kind uses, as {"kind": "key", "key": "A", "pressed": true} — send the release as a second event, or the key stays down. An event that leaves `pressed` out alternates on its own: the first is the press and the second the release, so a click is the same event written twice. A Button answers the release, not the press. A mouse_button event names its `button`, a joypad_button event its `joypadButton`, and a joypad_motion event its `axis`. A position is [x, y]. This drives the Input Map, so it is how you check that a level you built can actually be played. Its answer carries a frame, unless a later entry of the same call carries one too: a picture another picture replaces is not worth sending, and a moment in the middle of a key sequence is what capture is for.

params.name: events
params.note: Each event is {"kind": "key", "key": "A", "pressed": true}, and the release is a second event. The accepted names are the ones the schema's `key` lists.

entry.name: kind
entry.note: Which of the five an event is. Checked here rather than in the game: an event with no kind used to cross the socket and come back as `Input event kind '' is not supported`, which names nothing to send instead. One live turn wrote it 22 times.

entry.name: key
entry.note: The accepted names are the ones the schema's `key` lists.

entry.name: pressed
entry.note: Held down unless this says otherwise, so the release is a second event carrying false.

entry.name: button
entry.note: Which mouse button, for a mouse_button event.

entry.name: joypadButton
entry.note: Which joypad button, for a joypad_button event.

entry.name: axis
entry.note: Which joypad axis, for a joypad_motion event.

entry.name: value
entry.note: How far the axis is pushed, between -1 and 1.

operations.summary: Captures a PNG frame.

Lets the game run on for a few frames, then answers with how many passed and how long it took. A game that ends while you are waiting for it — a benchmark reaching the end of its work — answers `exited: true` instead of a frame count, rather than failing: the waiting is over either way, and the calls after this one still run. This is how you wait for something the game does over time — a tween, a timer, a unit walking somewhere — before capturing or inspecting it. Never wait by running `sleep` in bash: that stops this process rather than letting the game advance, and it costs a whole request to do nothing.

params.name: frames
params.note: How many rendered frames to let pass. One when neither this nor `ms` is named.

params.name: ms
params.note: How long to let pass instead, in milliseconds. Held under ten seconds, which is what one request has.

entry.name: exited
entry.note: True when the game was already gone, which is the answer a wait was run for.

operations.summary: Freezes the running game where it stands, the way its own pause menu would: `SceneTree.paused`, so a node that opted out of pausing keeps running. Use it before reading a game that moves — a path to a node a spawner made is stale as soon as that node is freed, and a frozen tree is one you can read twice. `resume` lets it go again. Gofer's own helper keeps answering either way.

alone.why: It takes no parameters, so a second one in the same call is the first one again.

operations.summary: Lets a paused game run on again.

alone.why: It takes no parameters, so a second one in the same call is the first one again.

operations.summary: Reads engine performance monitors. Without a list it answers with TIME_FPS, MEMORY_STATIC and OBJECT_NODE_COUNT; the names it accepts are the ones the schema lists, and any other name is an error.

entry.name: monitors
entry.note: Keyed by Performance.Monitor constant.

operations.summary: Reads a page. `editor` is the editor's stdout, which also carries what the game printed; `editorError` is where the engine reports its own failures, including a script that would not parse. Terminal colour is taken out, and the editor's own progress bar — `[  16% ] first_scan_filesystem | …` — is left out and counted in `terminalLinesOmitted`, because a terminal drawing itself is a fifth of this output and none of it is about the project. One line in `editorError` is never about the project: an `ERROR:` naming a section like `res://scripts/player.gd` with the key `state` is the editor restoring which script tabs were open. It is dropped from the errors a failed call carries, and left here because this is the raw page.

params.name: context
params.note: How many lines either side of each match to answer with. A banner is one matching line above the numbers it introduces, and asking for those by name only works when you already know their wording.

params.name: limit
params.note: How many matches to answer with, at most. The lines `context` asks for ride along and are not counted, so a page can never come back holding none of what was searched for.

operations.summary: Retrieves ranked passages for a question in plain words. Use it to see which chapters the manual has on a subject at all — when the question is which class to reach for, the list of chapters is the answer.

params.name: maxPassages
params.note: How many passages come back is not a number the model can reason about, so it is settled here at four. gofer-rag takes it as a ceiling and applies it before pinning a chapter the question named, so the rescue survives it; replaying its 83 labelled questions through every ceiling, four keeps 79% of the bytes and loses no case, where three loses two. The desktop Docs panel sets its own bound, so the parameter stays accepted and unadvertised.

operations.summary: Answers one question from those same passages and hands back a paragraph and a quote instead of the chapters. Use it when you want one fact — a signature, an argument, what a property does — and would only have read one line out of what `search` returns. The quote is checked against the manual: an answer that arrives with a warning that its quote is not there was written from memory, and is not evidence. It needs a model connection, where `search` does not.

params.name: maxPassages
params.note: How many passages come back is not a number the model can reason about, so it is settled here at four. gofer-rag takes it as a ceiling and applies it before pinning a chapter the question named, so the rescue survives it; replaying its 83 labelled questions through every ceiling, four keeps 79% of the bytes and loses no case, where three loses two. The desktop Docs panel sets its own bound, so the parameter stays accepted and unadvertised.
